41	**Requirements & Design:** 
42	
43	Some of our key design decisions this sprint (each is documented in more detail in the linked PR description):
44	
45	* Icon size as its own setting, separate from font size ([\#53](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/53), [PR 84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84), sgstrick)  
46	* Upstream sync through a reviewed merge branch ([\#95](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/95), [PR 99](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/99), bennettmatuszewski).   
47	* Fixing the Windows EBUSY test failure in the migration, not the test cleanup ([\#98](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/98)/[\#94](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/94), [PR 104](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/104), bennettmatuszewski).  
48	* Account colors stored as database columns and shown as tag-style pills ([\#24](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/24), [PR 112](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/112), bennettmatuszewski).  
49	* CI on GitHub-hosted runners while keeping upstream’s workflows ([\#101](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/101), [PR 113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113), TigerK9).  
50	* Fixing subcategory report totals without redesigning the graphs ([\#100](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/100), [PR 128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128), jamesleonard3rd).  
51	* Bulk schedule actions run as a loop on the client ([\#65](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/65), [PR 129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129), jamesleonard3rd).  
52	* Not tracking popover hover at all when the sidebar is pinned ([\#118](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/118), [PR 132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132), TigerK9).   
53	* A fixed “\#” prefix on the tag color hex input ([\#66](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/66), [PR 136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136), icsasso).   
54	* Live color preview, but save only when a change settles ([\#67](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/67), [PR 144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144), icsasso, still in review).   
55	* Verifying layouts with Playwright E2E tests and screenshots ([\#70](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/70), [PR 140](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/140), sgstrick).

76	**Test Strategy:**
77	
78	Getting CI working came first this sprint. Before [PR 113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113), CI had never run on our PRs, because the upstream workflows used Depot runners that are blocked on our repo, and that let lint errors, stale screenshots and a broken E2E test reach master. After moving CI to GitHub-hosted runners, we fixed the failures that had piled up: [PR 115](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/115) fixed lint, formatting and knip,  [PR 116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116) regenerated 69 out-of-date visual regression (VRT) screenshots, [PR 132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) fixed the bug behind the failing “schedules” E2E test, and [PR 104](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/104) fixed tests that failed locally (Windows file locks, Vitest picking up Stryker’s leftover .stryker-tmp copies, and an i18n race in mutations.test.tsx). From then on, every PR got lint, typecheck, unit, E2E and VRT checks automatically.  
79	The tests we wrote fell into four groups:
80	
81	* Unit and component tests (Vitest). These were the most common. [PR 84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84) tested saving and loading the icon size preference, the default fallback and the pixel size for each multiplier. [PR 128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128) added subcategories.test.ts and showActivity.test.ts to check that unchecked subcategories are left out of custom reports. [PR 132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) added three pinned-sidebar tests using fake timers, including a regression test for the original bug, and updated three existing tests. [PR 136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136) added six tests for the hex input. PRs [124](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/124) and [130](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/130) added AI-generated unit tests for the net worth percentage and personal inflation features.  
82	* End-to-end tests (Playwright). [PR 129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129) added tests for bulk skip, complete and delete, select-all, completed rows having no checkbox, and clicking a row still opening the editor. [PR 140](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/140) added layout tests at four viewport widths across three themes, plus a sweep across 19 widths, and recorded two known layout bugs with test.fail() so they turn into regression tests once fixed.  
83	* Visual regression tests. Baselines were regenerated wherever a PR changed the UI ([PR 116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116), [PR 128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128), [PR 129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129)).  
84	* Mutation testing (Stryker). In [PR 112](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/112), the changed code scored 100%, and each killed mutant was checked to be a real test failure. Stryker’s Vitest runner ran 0 tests on Windows and parallel runs crashed, so it had to be run one mutant at a time with temporary configs.
85	
86	Every PR was also tested by hand in the running app, and several ([128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128), [130](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/130), [136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136), [144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)) included step-by-step instructions so the reviewer could reproduce the check.

89	
90	- **Liam:** For this sprint I used AI in a very similar manner to Sprint 1\. I used Claude Code as an extension in Visual Studio, and used specstory to log them in my ai-logs like before. For PR descriptions and review comments, I would have AI type out responses, then I’d take the time to rewrite responses in my own words, though I didn’t always do this. I’d like to take more time to rewrite what Claude outputs so that I understand exactly what is being output and why. Something I did in this sprint that I didn’t do before was to push back on a lot of the outputs. Claude would tell me we should do something one way, and I’d realize it wouldn’t follow the structure of our project, or was too far out of the scope of the issue being worked on, and I’d bring the agent back in. I worked on four PRs, three of which I used AI to help me code and understand the project structure more. I also had it help me create my UML and Class diagrams during one of those sessions. I also used AI to review my teammates' code, giving one session to each PR reviewed. The other times I used AI were to create more extensive issue descriptions for my teammates to more easily implement their issues. **File location and format**

**Required sections**
1. **Team:** team name, member names and GitHub usernames, project name, and repository link.
2. **Sprint overview:** what the team planned, what it delivered, and an honest account of scope changes.
3. **Sprint backlog:** link to the Sprint 1 GitHub Milestone and a table of issues (title, owner, estimated points, scope, status). Include the rationale for how the sprint was scoped.
4. **Requirements and design:** whether specs were complete before coding, any surprises, and key design decisions with rationale.
5. **Completed issues:** a table of issue title, owner, and every associated PR (link, author, reviewers, status), plus a brief description of each change.
6. **Test strategy:** the kinds of tests written, and any changes that could not be tested automatically and why.
7. **AI tool usage:** for each member, the tools used, number of sessions logged, and a link to `ai-logs/sprint1/<username>/`. Also note patterns compared with Sprint 0. Each member gets 2–3 sentences on what worked well or what they would change.

9. **Risks and retrospective:** what went well, what slowed the team down, and what to do differently in Sprint 2.
10. **Sprint 2 plan:** initial ideas and any Sprint 1 issues to carry over.

**Grading**
- D6 is worth 10 points and is graded as a team on completeness, specificity, and quality of evidence.
- A team with no sprint report receives 0 for Sprint 1, regardless of other deliverables.
- The report also serves as the summary location for D1 (scoping rationale), D4 (PR links and summary table), D5 (AI log summary), and D7 (release link).

**Forward-looking requirements**
- The Sprint 2 plan section is the only report requirement that looks ahead.
- The Oct 20 Lightning Talk covers both Sprints 1 and 2. Its requirements are posted on the Presentations page, not in this section.

79	Sprint 2: Project Development & Quality¶
80	Oct 13-Oct 29 · All deliverables due Oct 29, 11:59 PM (with Mid-sprint check-in on Oct 22) · 100 points (10% of course grade)
81	Sprint 2 builds on Sprint 1: the goal is to further develop the system with new features, enhacements, defect corrections, etc. The issue backlog, PR workflow, and general expectations carry forward; see Sprint 1 for anything not explicitly changed here. This page covers what is new or different in Sprint 2.
82	Unfamiliar with a term?
83	Check the Glossary for definitions of terms used throughout this page.
84	Before you begin¶
85	Identify incomplete issues from Sprint 1. Review your unfinished Sprint 1 issues before selecting new work (see D1).
86	Read the "Things that must improve" section section below before starting D2-D5. These issues were observed in Sprint 1 and will be graded strictly.
87	Verify your AI log setup is working before starting new agentic sessions.
88	What is new in Sprint 2¶
89	UML diagrams and Q&A (D6): a new individual deliverable
90	Mid-sprint check-in (D7): a new individual deliverable, due Oct 22
91	Technical debt annotation: a required section in every PR description (D4)
92	Alternatives required in design decisions (D3)
93	Things that must improve from Sprint 1¶
94	These issues were observed in Sprint 1 and will be graded strictly in Sprint 2. If you are having issues with AI logging, please contact us promptly for support.
95	1. AI log completeness. Every student must have logs committed to the repo. Logs must include full session content: the prompts you wrote and the AI output in response. Summaries of conversations are not AI logs and will not receive full credit. AI output without the prompts that produced it are incomplete logs and will not receive full credit.
96	2. AI log linking. For every issue or PR that involved AI use, post a comment on that issue or PR (note: in this sprint we accept both AI log references in the issue or PR) that links directly to the specific log file. "Directly" means a link that opens the log file itself, not a link to the folder that contains it (e.g., ai-logs/sprint2/username/) and not a link to a different issue or PR. Use the format and template from AI Log Instructions -- you just require copy/pasting the template and changing the fields.
97	3. AI log format. SpecStory format is strongly recommended. Screenshots of the AI interface are not AI logs. Common mistakes to avoid:
98	Summaries of conversations instead of full output
99	Logs not linked from the issue or PR they document
100	AI output pasted without the prompts that produced it
101	4. No self-reviews. A student cannot approve or merge their own PR. Reviewers must post substantive comments, not just click approve. When your PR is ready for review, notify your reviewer promptly in your team's Zulip channel (or email). Aim to turn around reviews within 24 hours of being asked. Responsive code review is part of being a good team member.
102	5. Design decisions must include alternatives. Document at least two concrete options you considered and explain why you chose one over the other. "We decided to use X" without alternatives will not earn full credit.

137	D6 - UML Diagrams and Q&A (new)¶
138	This is a new individual deliverable.
139	Before drawing your diagrams, review the tutorials linked below. They explain UML elements, their meaning, and when to use each type of relationship or notation. Familiarity with the basics will make your diagrams significantly more accurate.
140	What to create: One class diagram and one sequence diagram for one of your medium issues. The person who resolved the issue creates the diagrams. The diagrams should show  code components and behavior relevant to your issue(s) --- more details below. Below we provide reference diagrams to guide this task.
141	If you resolved multiple small issues equivalent in scope to one medium issue
142	Create diagrams that cover all of those issues together.
143	The Gitea team (Go)
144	Both diagrams are required. Go uses structs and interfaces rather than classes; your class diagram should reflect Go's model (structs, interfaces, embedding). Include a brief note in your submission explaining the mapping from Go constructs to UML notation.
145	UML notation: Inheritance, composition, aggregation, dependency, and association are all valid and expected relationships for class diagrams (see the Glossary for definitions). For attributes and methods, show only those relevant to the issue; you do not need to show every member of every class.
146	Tutorials:
147	Class diagrams: Lucidchart -- How to Draw a UML Class Diagram
148	Sequence diagrams: Visual Paradigm -- Creating Sequence Diagrams · Gliffy -- UML Sequence Diagram Tutorial
149	Tools: To create the diagrams, you can use any tool of your preference. Examples: PlantUML, Mermaid (renders directly in GitHub Markdown), draw.io, Lucidchart, Visual Paradigm.
150	What the diagrams should show:
151	Each diagram should cover two things:
152	Relevant existing code you identified during concept location and impact analysis: the classes, components, or interactions already in the codebase that you needed to understand to implement your solution.
153	New and modified code that makes up your solution: the classes, methods, or interactions you added or changed.
154	Distinguish between existing and new/modified elements (for example, with a legend, color, or a label).
155	Annotations are required. Add brief notes directly on the diagram to explain key design decisions: why a specific relationship exists, why you structured a class a certain way, what an important method call is doing. Annotations are part of the deliverable and will be graded. Diagrams without annotations will not earn full credit. See the amber boxes in the reference diagrams below for examples of annotations.
156	Reference examples:
157	The examples below illustrate the expected style, level of detail, and annotation approach.
158	Example class diagram with annotated design decisions.
159	Example sequence diagram with annotated interactions.

176	**Class diagram:**
177	1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.
178	2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.
179	3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?
180	**Sequence diagram:**
181	1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?
182	2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.
183	3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?
184	**Cross-cutting:**
185	4. If you used AI to create or check any part of the diagrams, describe what it produced, what you verified against the actual code, and what you had to correct or add. If AI was not used, write "N/A."

73-Sprint 1 — Project Development & Release¶
74-Sep 22–Oct 8 · All deliverables due Oct 8, 11:59 PM · 100 points (10% of course grade)
75-Sprint 1 is the first full development sprint. By the end, each team should have a working release with new features and other changes that improve the project in a meaningful, demonstrable way. 
76-Each team will define the sprint backlog: prioritize, estimate, and select issues that will be solved in the sprint. Each team member will implement at least two medium-size issues (graduate students will implement at least an additional small issue) following the SE practices defined in Sprint 0.
77-Unfamiliar with a term in these instructions?
78-Check the Glossary for definitions of acceptance criteria, sprint backlog, release, CI, and other concepts used throughout this page.
79-Before you begin¶
80-Review your Sprint 0 deliverables before planning Sprint 1:
81-Re-read your issue backlog (D2 from S0). Which issues are most impactful? Which are feasible in ~2.5 weeks?
82-Re-read your standards document (D3 from S0). Conventions carry forward; update it if Sprint 0 revealed gaps.
83-Check the Sprint 0 report's "Sprint 1 ideas" section — treat it as a starting point.
84-Make sure all Sprint 0 PRs are merged and the repo is in a clean state before starting new work.
85-Make sure all Sprint 0 issues are closed (or explicitly marked as deferred).
86-Verify your AI log setup from Sprint 0 is working before starting new sessions.
87-Deliverables¶
88-D1 — Sprint Backlog (GitHub Issues)¶
89-The team selects and prepares the issues it will implement in Sprint 1.
90-Start this early. Issues may turn out to be broader than expected, overlap with each other, or be invalid. Discovering this in week 2 leaves no time to recover.
91-Step 1 — Refine the backlog. Go through all open issues as a team. Add missing ones, close invalid or duplicate ones, and decompose any large or XL issues into smaller sub-issues that can be completed within the sprint. Record decisions in a team meeting (preferred) or Zulip thread.
92-Step 2 — Estimate and select. Use the prioritization and estimation techniques from the planning lecture (story points and planning poker) to size and rank your backlog. Use any units for the story points. Select a set of issues the full team can realistically complete in 2.5 weeks. Your sprint backlog must meet the following minimums:
93-Role
94-Minimum issues selected
95-Each CSCI 435 member
96-at least 2 medium issues (or equivalent story points)
97-Each CSCI 535 (grad) member
98-at least 2 medium issues + 1 additional small issue (or equivalent story points)
99-Quality over quantity
100-One well-implemented, thoroughly tested feature is worth more than three half-finished ones. Plan conservatively, then expand if you're ahead of schedule.
101-GitHub Projects
102-Consider using GitHub Projects to organize your backlog, track progress, and visualize point burndown. It integrates directly with your issues and milestone. See the GitHub for Beginners tutorial — the Projects section starts at 02:59 in the accompanying video. Try the Team planning or Kanban templates; Team planning supports custom fields such as estimated story points.
103-Step 3 — Assign ownership. Every selected issue must have a single owner (assigned in GitHub). One issue per member at minimum; members may own more than one. No issue should be assigned to more than one person.
104-Step 4 — Create the Sprint 1 milestone. Create a GitHub Milestone named Sprint 1 and attach all selected issues to it.
105-Instructor and TA involvement
106-The instructor or TA may add new issues or flag specific issues as high priority during the sprint. Treat this as the customer expressing urgency — acknowledge it and adjust your plan accordingly.
107-Suggested pacing
108-Aim to have issue specs written and peer-reviewed (see D2) by Sep 27. That leaves a bit more than 1.5 weeks for implementation with clear targets in hand. If specs are still being drafted next week, you are likely behind.
109:What to provide in D6 (Sprint report): Link to the Sprint 1 milestone; brief rationale for how you scoped the sprint.
110-D2 — Requirements Specification¶
111-For each issue in your Sprint 1 backlog, the owner must write or significantly refine the specification before writing any code.
112-Format: If your project already uses an issue template, adapt it to include the fields below. If your project has no feature request template, create one. Otherwise, use the following structure as a guide.
113-For features and enhancements, write the issue as a user story that satisfies the INVEST criteria -- see also the slides on Project management:
114-## User Story
115-As a [type of user], I want [goal] so that [benefit].
116-## User Scenario
117-[A concrete walkthrough of how a user encounters and uses this feature.]
118-## Acceptance Criteria
119-1. ...
120-2. ...
121-3. ...
122-## Out of Scope
123-- ...
124-## Open Questions
125-- ...
126-Each acceptance criterion must be testable — observable behavior, not vague intent. Minimum 3 per issue.
127-What makes a criterion testable?
128-A testable criterion has a clear pass/fail outcome: "The export button is disabled when no items are selected" is testable. "The UI should feel responsive" is not. If you cannot write a test or manual step that definitively passes or fails it, rewrite it.
129-For bug reports, include at minimum:
130-## Observed Behavior (OB)
131-[What currently happens.]
132-## Expected Behavior (EB)
133-[What should happen instead.]
134-## Steps to Reproduce (S2R)
135-1. ...
136-2. ...
137-## Additional Information
138-[Screenshots, stack traces, error logs — recommended.]
139-Before finalizing your spec, have at least one teammate read it and leave a comment on the issue confirming it is clear enough to implement. This is a lightweight requirements review.
140-Submission: All issue specs updated in GitHub. Links included in D6.
141-D3 — Design Decisions¶
142-For each issue in your Sprint 1 backlog, the owner must document at least one non-trivial design decision before or during implementation.
143-What to document:
144-Field
145-Description
146-Decision
147-One sentence stating what you decided
148-Alternatives considered
149-At least two concrete options you evaluated
150-Rationale
151-Why you chose this option over the others
152-Consequences
153-What this decision makes easier and what it makes harder
154-Where to put it: Add a ## Design section to the GitHub issue body, in an issue comment, or include it in the PR description. For decisions that affect multiple issues or the overall architecture, add a team-level note to docs/sprint1/design.md.
155-Don't overthink the scope
156-"Should I add this field to the existing component or create a new one?" with a clear rationale is a perfectly good design decision. The goal is to make your reasoning visible — one sentence per field is enough. This is not a design document.

Submission: Design decisions documented in GitHub issues, PR descriptions, or docs/sprint1/design.md. Links in D6.
D4 — Code Changes and Pull Requests¶
This is the core development activity of Sprint 1. Each team member implements their assigned issue(s) through the full PR workflow.
At least one PR per issue must be created, merged, and closed. In most cases, one issue maps to one PR; if an issue truly requires multiple PRs, split it into sub-issues first.
Requirements for each PR:
Linked to a GitHub issue (Closes #<number> in the description).
Description clearly explains what changed, why, and how it was tested.
New or updated tests for every behavioral change; test strategy explained in the PR.
CI should pass if it is configured for your project. If CI is not yet working, document manual verification in the PR description instead — CI setup is encouraged but not required for all projects.
Reviewed by at least one teammate (not yourself) using the code review rubric below — same process as Sprint 0.
Merged before the sprint deadline.
Delete the branch after the PR is merged (same as Sprint 0).
Code review rubric:
When a PR is ready for review, the reviewer must evaluate it on the criteria below and post the filled-in rubric as a comment on the PR. Fill in the rubric during your initial review pass — before the author makes any revisions in response to your comments. Scoring it after all back-and-forth fixes defeats the purpose. If you review a follow-up revision, you may add a brief update to your comment noting what changed.
The Notes column should include a brief explanation (one to two sentences) of your score. Reviewers may also make specific comments on individual lines of code via GitHub's code review interface.
Criterion
Score (1–10)
Notes
Correctness — does the change do what the issue asked?
Test coverage — are tests present and meaningful?
Code quality — consistent style, clear naming, no unnecessary duplication
Documentation — inline comments and PR description are clear
AI transparency — if AI was used, is there evidence of human verification?
Overall — would you merge this as-is?
Use this template for your review comment:
## Code Review
| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness — does the change do what the issue asked? | | |
| Test coverage — are tests present and meaningful? | | |
| Code quality — consistent style, clear naming, no unnecessary duplication | | |
| Documentation — inline comments and PR description are clear | | |
| AI transparency — if AI was used, is there evidence of human verification? | | |
| Overall — would you merge this as-is? | | |
Each student must conduct at least one code review per sprint. Over the course of the semester, each student must review code from every teammate at least once.
Before you write any code:
Read the issue and spec. Understand the acceptance criteria before touching any code.
Consider using AI. If you find an agentic tool helpful, use it to validate, extend, or accelerate your understanding — but you must be able to explain every line in your PR.
You must be able to explain every line
Reviewers and the instructor may ask you to explain any part of your change at any time. If you cannot, you will receive points off.
Using AI more intentionally
Before accepting a proposed change, ask the agent to explain what it changed and why, and what could go wrong. This keeps you engaged with the change before it lands in your branch — and gives you something concrete to say during code review.
Branch and PR workflow (same as Sprint 0):
# Sync with main before starting
git checkout main
git pull origin main
# Create a branch for your issue
git checkout -b feat/issue-42-export-pdf   # new feature
git checkout -b fix/issue-17-date-overflow  # bug fix
# After making changes and running tests:
git add <changed files>
git commit -m "feat: add PDF export for reports (#42)"
git push origin feat/issue-42-export-pdf
After pushing, open the PR via GitHub's "Compare & pull request" banner. Select main as the base branch.
After your PR is merged, clean up:
git checkout main           # switch back to main
git pull origin main        # pull the merged changes
git branch -d feat/issue-42-export-pdf  # delete local branch (safe: only works if merged)
Also delete the remote branch from GitHub: on the merged PR page, click "Delete branch".
Submission: All PRs merged. Links and a summary table in D6.
D5 — AI Logs¶
Continue the logging practice from Sprint 0. Every agentic session related to Sprint 1 work must be logged. The requirements below are stricter than Sprint 0 — review them carefully before submitting.
Where to store logs: ai-logs/sprint1/<your-github-username>/
Naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md — e.g., 2026-09-25_claude-code_issue-42-pdf-export.md. Follow the same convention described in AI Log Instructions.
Format requirements:
Logs must capture full session metadata: timestamps, prompts, and AI responses. Use SpecStory or a browser export extension when available (see AI Log Instructions). If no export tool exists for your tool, manually transcribe the session with every message labeled [User] or [AI] and include timestamps. Do not submit raw, unstructured copy-pastes. Accepted formats: .md (preferred), .txt, .json.
Do not summarize or reconstruct your AI usage after the fact. Logs must be captured during the session.
Do not submit .html, .docx, or .pdf log files, or links to private chats. These will not receive credit.
Linking: Reference your log files in a comment on the corresponding GitHub issue — do not add AI log references to the PR description. Use the format and template described in AI Log Instructions. Logs not linked to an issue comment will not receive credit. Broken links will not receive credit.
Log references go in issue comments only
Logs may be committed to the repo via a PR, but the reference must still appear in an issue comment — not in the PR description or in a PR comment. Each contributor (implementor, code reviewer, estimator) posts their own comment on the issue — if three people worked on an issue, there should be three separate AI Assistance comments.
If you did not use AI for an issue, post a brief note in an issue comment stating this. No log file is needed for that issue, but your log folder must still exist.
What to include in D6: Per member: tools used, number of sessions logged, link to ai-logs/sprint1/<username>/, and 2–3 sentences on what worked well or what you'd do differently.
Submission: Logs pushed to the repo. Summary in D6.

Despite not completing every issue we set out to do in the milestone, we learned from this to set more achievable goals for ourselves that are doable in a given sprint rather than trying to fit more than we can handle into a small time-frame.

52-## Requirements & Design
53-
54-In all cases, specs were completed before coding started. We made sure to add user stories, acceptance criteria, etc. and update all issues to be more detailed. This made it easier when actually implementing these issues as there was more detail and clear criteria for what the change set out to do. We were surprised at how long it can take to draft up these specific specs for each issue, but we believe it was worth it for the clarity adding specifications to each issue provided. Our PRs this sprint required many more design decisions compared to Sprint 0, as we were working on bigger tasks. For each issue there were many open questions that had to be decided, such as "where should this feature live?" and "what should happen if the user does this?". We also had to make design decisions inside of the codebase. For example, in the codebase there are often many ways to approach one issue and many ways to implement it. We tried our best to write as clean code as possible and look at existing implementations before diving in, to ensure our code remains consistent with the existing codebase.
55-
56-Some of our key design decisions this sprint:
57-
58-- **PDF export ([#76](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/76)):** We split the original issue and only implemented downloading the PDF, deferring layout polish to a later issue. jsPDF only supports Latin characters by default, so supporting non-Latin currency symbols would have made the PR too large to review well.
59-- **Shared export logic ([#75](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/75)):** CSV and PDF exports use the same data-building module, so both formats always contain the same numbers.
60-- **Subcategories ([#73](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/73)):** Money for a subcategory always comes out of its parent's budget and is capped at what the parent has, rather than coming straight from "To Budget". This keeps totals and "To Budget" correct without changing how the rest of the budget works.
61-- **Personal Goal widget ([#87](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/87)):** We chose a dedicated goal page for full setup, with quick edits available on the card itself, so the card stays simple while still allowing detailed configuration.
62-- **Floating sidebar ([#79](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/79)):** The floating sidebar now shares the same container as the main content, so the page resizes when the sidebar opens instead of the sidebar covering it.

## Sprint 2 Summary

Sprint 2 added new reporting features and customization options, fixed several UI and report bugs, and made the CI pipeline more reliable.

### New features
- **Personal inflation report:** a new report and dashboard widget showing your personal inflation rate (#130)
- **Net worth percentage change:** the net worth report and widget now show percentage change (#124)
- **Bulk edit schedules:** edit several schedules at once (#129)
- **Adjustable icon sizes:** a new option to change icon sizes (#53, #84)
- **Tag color picker:** a live hex color preview and a fixed "#" prefix (#136)
- **Account colors:** account colors can now have a description (#112)

### Bug fixes
- Custom reports no longer count unchecked subcategories in their parent's total (#128)
- The pinned sidebar no longer closes context menus after you leave a popover (#132)

### Infrastructure and maintenance
- Synced with upstream Actual v26.10.0 (#99)
- Set up mutation testing with StrykerJS and fixed failing tests (#92, #104)
- CI now runs on GitHub-hosted runners, with lint/knip errors fixed and VRT screenshots updated (#113, #115, #116)
- Fixed the dev container (#103)

### Documentation
- UML diagrams with Q&A (#131, #143), layout verification (#140), mid-sprint check-ins, and release notes (#122)

## What's Changed
* Add Sprint 1 report by @TigerK9 in https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/90
* [AI] Set up StrykerJS mutation testing for loot-core budg
===== 84
(no Design heading) 
===== 99
## Design Decisions

1. Integration strategy: merge, not rebase

- **Chosen:** Merge upstream into a separate sync branch (`chore/sync-upstream-v26.10.0`), then open a PR into `master`.
- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Rebase the fork's commits onto upstream.** This rewrites the history of a shared `master` that teammates have already pulled, and it would force every teammate's open branch to be rebased.
  - **GitHub's "Sync fork" button.** It merges straight into `master` with no review step, can't resolve conflicts, and merges upstream's latest `master` instead of a release.
  - **Merge straight into local `master`.** That skips team review of 26 hand-resolved files.
- **Why:** A merge keeps existing history intact. The PR gives the team a chance to review the conflict resolutions before they land on `master`.

2. Merge target: the commit the release was built from

- **Chosen:** Upstream `master` at `bfa850ca6`, the commit the 26.10.0 release was built from. It was identified by comparing files: it matches the release except for 7 version-number lines.
- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **The `v26.10.0` release tag.** This was tried and aborted. The tag sits on a release branch of squashed copies of commits, which produced dozens of fake conflicts.
  - **The latest upstream `master` (Oct 16).** It would have brought in three weeks of unreleased, less-tested work and made "we're on 26.10.0" untrue.
- **Why:** It's the released code, and it shares history with the fork, so only real conflicts appear.


===== 104
## Design Decisions

- **The database is closed in the migration, not the test cleanup.** A real down migration on Windows would hit the same `EBUSY` error, so fixing it in the migration covers both cases.
- **The connection is reset after it's closed.** `closeAccountDb()` clears the stored connection, so the next `getAccountDb()` call opens a fresh one instead of reusing a closed one.
- **The change is kept small.** No test files or shared database code were changed. Only the database that blocks the folder delete gets closed.


===== 112
## Design Decisions

1. **Where to store the description**
   - *Options:* (a) a new `description` column on `accounts`; (b) reuse the existing account Notes (the `notes` table, keyed `account-<id>`).
   - *Chose (a).* The ticket models the feature on tags, which have a short `description` field.
     - A column goes through `account-update`, so it can be undone, syncs per field, and can be queried through AQL.
     - Notes are long Markdown text in a popover, and saving them can't be undone.
     - The cost is two similar text fields on an account.

2. **How to store the color**
   - *Options:* (a) an additive SQL migration adding nullable `color` and `description` columns; (b) a synced preference per account (e.g. `account-<id>-color`), like the existing `show-account-<id>-net-worth-chart`.
   - *Chose (a).* Every screen that already loads accounts gets the color with no extra query.
     - Changes can be undone and are part of `AccountEntity`.
     - The migration follows the repo's additive-only rule.
     - Preferences can't be undone and would need a separate lookup in every table that shows accounts.

3. **How the color looks in tables**
   - *Options:* (a) a pill like tags; (b) a colored dot before the name; (c) the name itself in the account color.
   - *Chose (a).* It matches tags, as the ticket asks, and reuses their black-or-white text contrast logic.
     - Colored text is hard to read for very light or dark colors in some themes.
     - A dot is easy to miss when scanning for patterns.

4. **What the pill is**
   - *Options:* (a) a non-interactive `<span>`; (b) a `<Button>`, as tag pills use.
   - *Chose (a).* Clicks pass through to the table cell, so clicking an account on All Accounts still opens the dropdown as before, as the tic
===== 113
## Design

**Decision:** Keep upstream's workflows, but swap their Depot runner labels to GitHub-hosted Linux runners in the PR checks we need, turn off upstream-only jobs with an `if: github.repository == 'actualbudget/actual'` guard, and add a fork-only check that fails if a Depot label comes back.

**Alternatives considered:**
1. **Swap labels everywhere:** change every `depot-*` label in all workflow files to its GitHub equivalent, including publishing and release workflows. Simple, but it would have let publish jobs actually run here (for example, the nightly Docker build would push images to our GitHub registry), and nothing would stop upstream syncs from quietly adding new Depot jobs.
2. **Write our own CI file:** turn off every inherited workflow and add one fork-owned workflow that runs lint, typecheck, unit tests and build. Easiest to understand, but we would lose upstream's E2E and visual regression tests and every future improvement to them.
3. **Self-hosted runner or paying for Depot:** register our own machine under the `depot-*` labels, or buy a Depot plan. A self-hosted runner on a public repo runs any PR's code on that machine, which GitHub warns against, and Depot costs money without giving us anything GitHub's free runners don't.

**Rationale:** Our repo is public, so GitHub-hosted runners are free and about as fast as the Depot machines upstream used for most jobs. Keeping upstream's workflows means we keep its full test suite. Guard lines turn off upstream-only jobs in code (no team member has admin access to turn them off in settings) and match a pattern upstream already uses. GitHub doesn't mark our repo as a fork, so upstream's own fork checks didn't protect us. We ran Linux only to keep CI fast and simple.

## Design Decisions

- **Keep subcategories rolled into the parent's bar, and only fix which ones are included.** The issue also asks to see how much each subcategory contributes. This PR doesn't change the graphs, so it stays small and fixes the incorrect totals first. Two alternatives were considered:
  1. **Show each subcategory as its own bar.**
     - Pros: fits every graph type.
     - Cons: needs a new saved report option (database migration, report types, sidebar toggle, dashboard widgets), plus click-through changes in five graph components. Without a toggle it would change how every existing report looks.
     - Status: left as a follow-up.
  2. **Split each parent's bar into coloured segments, one per subcategory.**
     - Pros: looks good for Bar, and possibly Donut.
     - Cons: doesn't carry over to Stacked Bar (which already stacks categories over time), Line or Area, so behaviour would be inconsistent across graph types. Also needs per-segment data, colours, tooltips, legend and click handling, and new visual regression snapshots. It wouldn't fix the totals on its own either; this PR's filter change is still needed underneath.
- **The checkbox filter is applied as written instead of expanding parents.** Ticking a parent already ticks all its subcategories, so the filter already lists exactly what's checked. Expanding it was what added unchecked subcategories back. Other category filters, and other reports such as Spending and Cash Flow, still include a parent's subcategories.
- **A subcategory checked without its parent gets its own row.** Showing it under a parent the user unchecked was misleading. Hiding it would have dropped data the user asked for.
- **The click-through query isn't changed.** It still asks for the parent and all its subca

## Design Decisions

- **Bulk actions run in a loop on the client, calling the existing single-schedule action once per selected schedule.** This reuses the server methods the row menu already calls, so the behaviour of each action is unchanged and no `loot-core` code changes. One alternative was considered:
  1. **Edit all selected schedules at once with batch server methods** (e.g. `schedule/delete-all`, following the existing `rule-delete-all`).
     - Pros: one request per bulk action instead of one per schedule, the data refreshes once, and a single undo reverts the whole bulk action.
     - Cons: needs four new server methods with types and tests. Posting a transaction and skipping a date each run per-schedule logic (rules, next-date calculation) that would have to be restructured to run in a batch.
     - Status: left as a follow-up if undoing one schedule at a time proves to be a problem.
- **Completed schedules have no checkbox.** The issue says completed schedules can't be bulk-edited, and leaving out the checkbox enforces that without extra rules in the menu. One alternative was considered:
  1. **Let completed schedules be selected, and disable or hide the actions that don't apply to them**, offering Restart when only completed schedules are selected.
     - Pros: would also allow bulk restarting or deleting completed schedules.
     - Cons: editing completed schedules is out of scope for the issue. Mixed selections would need rules for which actions to show, and select-all would have to decide whether to include completed schedules hidden behind "Show completed schedules".
     - Status: not done.
- **Only visible, active schedules can be selected.** The selection is given only the schedules matching the search filter that aren't completed. Sele

## Design decisions

1. AI helped me come up with the three following ways for how to fix the original issue:

A. Only add the floating check to the close effect.
B. Don't attach the listener when pinned, and add the check (chosen).
C. Close menus from inside the hide timer instead of an effect.

We ended up picking B: it removed the cause, so a pinned sidebar doesn't track hover nor re-renders every useSiderbar consumer. This doesn't touch floating mode. A leaves the pointless state changes in place. C restructures the code and changes how the touch toggle behaves.

2. Scope:
Also fix floating-mode menu ownership (a data-sidebar attribute plus checking where the contextmenu event came from, or an owner field in Redux). We fixed pinned mode only; the issue is estimated small, and this PR is blocking CI, so it should stay small.

3. Keep the floating check on the close effect even though the listener is skipped when pinned, rather than relying on the listener alone. It stops a stray close if someone switches from floating to pinned mid-hover, and a test covers that case.

4. Tests:
A setup line in each affected test. 
Reorganize into `pinned` / `floating` `describe` blocks.
I did this because the per-test line keeps the diff small and easy to review.

===== 140
## Design Decisions
I decided to keep this PR as simply creating unit tests and creating a new issue rather than trying to solve the issue here. The narrow-viewport size shown below is an issue deemed outside the scope, to be fixed in a later issue.

In regards to the unit tests:
**1. Used playwright e2e tests instead of unit tests.** Alternatives: Vitest component tests, or unit tests of the width logic. Rationale: Vitest runs in jsdom, which doesn't calculate layout, so overflow and clipping can't be measured; unit tests would pass while the real page overflows. Consequence: slower tests (about 2 minutes for the section) that need a running dev server, but they catch real rendering problems.
**2. Code checks plus screenshots.** Alternatives: screenshots only, or code checks only. Rationale: screenshots alone can approve an image that already contains a bug and don't name the broken element, while code checks alone miss visual problems they weren't written for. Consequence: 21 snapshots to maintain, generated in Docker or with `/update-vrt`.
**3. Amounts cut short with "…" count as failures.** Alternatives: allow ellipsis truncation, or check only for sideways page scrolling. Rationale: a truncated amount hides digits, and the page-level check missed every problem we found because the table clips its contents instead of making the page scroll. Consequence: stricter than the current UI, which exposed the 668–749px problem; vertical clipping isn't checked.
**4. Screenshots at four widths, plus a sweep without screenshots.** Alternatives: screenshots at every width, or fixed widths only. Rationale: screenshots at every width would mean hundreds of snapshots, and fixed widths alone couldn't find the 750px threshold. Consequence: the sweep adds about 28 seconds and depends 
===== 144
## Design
| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| Decision | Keep the live preview separate from saving. Every color change is written straight into the cached list of tags, with no database write, so all visible tags recolor live. The color is saved (`updateTag`) only once a change is settled, through a new `onChangeEnd` prop on `ColorPicker`. A change counts as settled when a swatch is picked, a complete hex code is entered, a drag ends, or a held key is released. |
| Alternatives Considered | **B:** throttle or debounce `updateTag` to about 150 ms. **C:** an explicit Apply/Cancel button. |
| Rationale | Saving on every `onChange` would flood the database and the sync server with writes while dragging, and tags would flicker as refetches overlap. "B" still records intermediate colors in sync history. "C" adds an extra click and behaves differently from swatches, which apply instantly. "A" satisfies the "update in real time with existing tags" acceptance criterion with exactly one save per change. |
| Consequences | `ColorPicker` gained a new `onChangeEnd` prop, because react-aria's picker only provides `onChange`. Every keyboard step also counts as a settled change, so held keys had to be batched into a single save on release, and accelerated so they don't feel slow. If the popover closes mid-change, the pending color is saved when the picker closes. |

# Issue #96 rescope — drafts

Replace `#A` and `#B` with the real issue numbers once the sub-issues are filed.
#A and #B can be worked on at the same time. #B uses the helper and label that #A adds, so #B merges after #A.

---

## Parent: #96 (edit existing issue)

**Title:** Show when a report widget has unsaved changes

**Labels:** `scope: large`, `type: improvement`

### Summary

When you change a report's filters, date range or display options and then leave without pressing **Save widget**, Actual drops the changes, and nothing on the page tells you they were unsaved. Custom Reports already show "(modified)" next to the report name when they have unsaved edits; the other 13 dashboard widget reports don't. This epic adds the same "(modified)" label to every widget report, so users can see at a glance that they have something to save.

### User Story

As a budget user who customizes dashboard reports, I want to see when a report has unsaved changes so that I remember to press **Save widget** before leaving.

### Sub-issues

- [ ] #A — Show a "(modified)" label on the standard report widgets
- [ ] #B — Show a "(modified)" label on the Formula and experimental report widgets

### Scope

Large as a whole: 13 report pages each need their own change detection. It's split into two medium sub-issues.

### Source

While reviewing the goal-card widget PRs, I noticed that leaving the card without saving silently drops your changes. None of the other reports warn you either.

### Design

**Decision: show that changes are unsaved, instead of blocking the user from leaving.**

The original version of this issue proposed a "Save / Discard / Cancel" dialog that would appear whenever the user tried to leave a report with unsaved changes. We considered three options:

== # 119
## Design

**Decision:** Exclude `ai-logs/**` and `docs/**` from oxfmt with `ignorePatterns` in `.oxfmtrc.json`, and auto-fix only the source code.

**Alternatives considered:**

1. **Let oxfmt reformat everything, including `ai-logs/` and `docs/`.** This is the default behavior and needs no config change. Rejected because AI logs must be the verbatim captured sessions, and reformatting changes them after the fact. It also added a large, noisy diff unrelated to the fix.
2. **Revert the log and doc changes by hand in this PR and change no config.** Rejected because the next `yarn lint:fix` would rewrite them again, and the `lint` job would keep failing on those files.
3. **Turn off or make optional the `lint` job in CI.** Rejected because it hides real problems in source code.

**Rationale:** `ignorePatterns` is a one-line, config-level fix that protects our AI logs and sprint docs from every future formatter run. Source code stays fully checked.

**Consequences:**

- *Easier:* `yarn lint` and `yarn lint:fix` can run safely from the repo root. The `lint` job checks only code, so its failures are meaningful.
- *Harder:* Markdown under `docs/` is no longer format-checked, so inconsistent formatting there won't be caught. Our `.oxfmtrc.json` (and `knip.json`) now differ from upstream, which may cause merge conflicts during upstream syncs.

== # 120
## Design

**Decision:** Regenerate the snapshots with a temporary GitHub Actions workflow on the PR branch that copies the CI VRT environment, then delete the workflow before merge.

**Alternatives considered:**

1. **Generate snapshots locally in the dev container.** Fast and needs no workflow. Rejected because the dev container is Debian on arm64 without Docker, while CI runs Ubuntu jammy on x86_64. Font rendering differs, so with a 5-pixel tolerance the new baselines would very likely still fail CI.
2. **Adapt upstream's `/update-vrt` comment bot for our fork.** Reusable. Rejected for now because it is locked to `actualbudget/actual`, expects Depot runners and an `ACTIONS_UPDATE_TOKEN` secret, and only runs from `master`. Editing upstream's workflow files would also risk merge conflicts on every upstream sync.
3. **Add a permanent manually triggered "Update VRT snapshots" workflow to `master`.** Reusable from the Actions tab without touching upstream files. Deferred because it needs its own PR and review, and CI needed to be unblocked first.

**Rationale:** The temporary workflow produces screenshots that match CI pixel for pixel in a single run, using only the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`. It changes no upstream workflow files. It also catches every stale screenshot, including the ones hidden behind each test's first failure.

**Consequences:**

- *Easier:* CI is green, and the
== #11

## Sprint Overview

At the start of the sprint, the team met to plan how we would handle the new Sprint 2 requirements: the UML diagrams, the mid-sprint check-in, the Tech Debt section in every PR, and alternatives in every design decision. Everyone self-assigned existing backlog issues, and together we wrote 4 new medium issues so that every member had at least 2 medium issues (12 issues for 6 members).

The sprint grew to **16 issues**. Early on we found that CI had never actually run on our PRs, that our fork was behind upstream, and that several tests failed on master or on Windows machines. We added issues to fix CI, sync with upstream Actual v26.10.0, fix the failing tests, and add VRT screenshots to our PRs, because every feature PR depended on that work.

**What was delivered:** 15 of the 16 issues were completed and their PRs merged. The one exception is [#67](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/67) (custom color wheel, [PR #144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)). The PR is finished, but the reviewer requested changes, so it carries over to Sprint 3.

- **New features:** personal inflation report and widget, net worth percentage change, bulk editing of schedules, adjustable icon size, account colors and descriptions, and a live hex preview in the tag color picker.
- **Bug fixes:** custom reports no longer count unchecked subcategories, and context menus no longer close on their own when the sidebar is pinned.
- **Infrastructure:** CI now runs on every PR (lint, typecheck, unit, E2E and VRT), the fork is synced with upstream v26.10.0, and the test suite passes locally on Windows.

## Sprint Backlog

**Milestone:** [Sprint 2 milestone](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/milestone/2)

**How we read the columns.** _Owner_ is the person who created the issue and wrote its scope, requirements and estimate. _Assigned to_ is the person who implemented it. If the spec was missing details, the assignee added them before coding.

**Story points.** We use a 1–10 scale: 1–2 is small, 3–7 is medium and 8–10 is large. We started by estimating as a team, as in Sprint 1, but it took too long, so each issue's owner estimated it. A few issues were scoped by the whole team.

**Backlog rationale.**

- **Sprint 1 carryovers first.** Unfinished Sprint 1 work (#53, #24, #70) went into the backlog before any new work.
- **Scope minimum.** Each member then took at least 2 medium issues (or the equivalent in small issues). We wrote 4 new medium issues so there were enough to go around.
- **CI and maintenance issues were added mid-sprint.** Once CI was running, failures on master blocked every feature PR, so we added and fixed them: #101, #118, #119, #120, #94/#98 and #95. #119 and #120 were created after their PRs, to document CI fixes that were already in progress.

## Requirements & Design

**Were specs complete before coding?** For most issues, yes. Feature issues had a user story, user scenario, acceptance criteria and out-of-scope list, and bug issues had observed behavior, expected behavior and steps to reproduce, before work began. The exceptions were #119 and #120, which were created after their PRs to document CI fixes that had to happen immediately to unblock everyone else.

**Surprises:**

- **The upstream sync was much harder than expected.** It was estimated at 1 point. Merging the `v26.10.0` release tag produced dozens of false conflicts and had to be aborted. The final merge brought in 215 upstream commits and needed 25 conflicts resolved by hand.
- **CI had never run on any of our PRs.** Upstream's workflows use Depot runners, which are blocked on our repo. That meant lint errors, 69 outdated screenshots and a broken E2E test had reached master unnoticed.
- **#11 was smaller than estimated.** It was first estimated as large. Once we found that the YTD logic and starting balance already existed in `net-worth-spreadsheet.ts`, it was re-scoped to medium.
- **#70 found a real bug.** Its new layout tests found a narrow-screen bug between 668 and 749px, filed as [#139](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/139).

**Key design decisions.** Full details, including consequences, are in each linked issue or PR.

| Issue / PR | Decision | Alternatives considered | Why |
| :--------- | :------- | :---------------------- | :-- |
| [#53](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/53) / [PR 84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84) (sgstrick) | Icon size is its own setting, with fixed Small/Medium/Large options. | Let the user enter an exact size or scale for icons. | Fixed sizes can each be tested to fit in every page layout. An arbitrary size could break layouts. |
| [#95](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/95) / [PR 99](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/99) (bennettmatuszewski) | Merge upstream into a separate sync branch and open a reviewed PR. Target the upstream commit the 26.10.0 release was built from. | Rebase our commits onto upstream; GitHub's "Sync fork" button; merge the `v26.10.0` tag; merge upstream's latest `master`. | Rebasing would rewrite shared history. "Sync fork" has no review step. The tag produced false conflicts. Latest `master` included unreleased work. |
| [#94/#98](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/98) / [PR 104](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/104) (bennettmatuszewski) | Fix the Windows `EBUSY` error by closing the database in the migration. | Close it in the test cleanup instead. | A real down migration on Windows would hit the same error, so fixing the migration covers both. |
| [#24](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/24) / [PR 112](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/112) (bennettmatuszewski) | Store account color and description as new database columns, and show the color as a tag-style pill. | Reuse account Notes for the description; store the color as a per-account preference; show a colored dot or colored text. | Columns can be undone, sync and are loaded with every account. The pill matches tags and stays readable in every theme. |
| [#101](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/101) / [PR 113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113) (TigerK9) | Keep upstream's workflows, swap Depot runners for GitHub-hosted ones in the PR checks, and turn off upstream-only jobs. | Swap every runner label everywhere; write our own CI file; use a self-hosted runner or pay for Depot. | Keeps upstream's full E2E and VRT suite for free, without letting publish jobs run on our repo. |
| [#119](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/119) / [PR 115](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/115) (TigerK9) | Exclude `ai-logs/` and `docs/` from the formatter and auto-fix only source code. | Let the formatter rewrite everything; revert log changes by hand; turn off the lint job. | AI logs must stay verbatim. Turning off lint would hide real problems. |
| [#120](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/120) / [PR 116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116) (TigerK9) | Regenerate screenshots with a temporary workflow that copies CI's environment, then delete it before merging. | Generate them locally in the dev container; adapt upstream's `/update-vrt` bot; add a permanent workflow. | Local screenshots don't match CI's rendering. Upstream's bot only works on their repo. A permanent workflow is planned for Sprint 3. |
| [#118](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/118) / [PR 132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) (TigerK9) | Don't track popover hover at all when the sidebar is pinned. | Only add a "floating" check to the close effect; close menus from inside the hide timer. | Removes the cause instead of hiding it, and leaves floating mode untouched. |
| [#100](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/100) / [PR 128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128) (jamesleonard3rd) | Fix which subcategories are counted in parent totals without redesigning the graphs. | Show each subcategory as its own bar; split each parent bar into colored segments. | Both alternatives need large changes across five graph types and wouldn't fix the totals on their own. They are left as follow-ups. |
| [#65](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/65) / [PR 129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129) (jamesleonard3rd) | Run bulk schedule actions as a loop on the client, reusing the existing single-schedule actions. Completed schedules get no checkbox. | New batch server methods; letting completed schedules be selected and disabling actions that don't apply. | No `loot-core` changes, and each action behaves exactly as it already did. Editing completed schedules is out of scope. |
| [#66](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/66) / [PR 136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136) (icsasso) | A fixed, non-editable "#" prefix, with the input holding only the hex digits. | Keep "#" in the value and block deleting it. | Blocking Backspace/Delete at the start of the input has many easy-to-miss edge cases. |
| [#67](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/67) / [PR 144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144) (icsasso, in review) | Preview colors live, but save only when a change settles. | Debounce saves to about 150 ms; add an Apply/Cancel button. | Exactly one save per change. Debouncing still records in-between colors, and a button adds an extra click. |
| [#70](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/70) / [PR 140](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/140) (sgstrick) | Verify layouts with Playwright E2E tests plus screenshots. | Vitest component tests or unit tests of the width logic; screenshots only or code checks only. | Vitest's jsdom doesn't calculate layout, so overflow can't be measured. Screenshots alone can approve an image that already has a bug. |

### What each PR changed

**Features**

- **[PR #130](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/130) – Add personal inflation report and dashboard widget.** Adds a new report page and dashboard widget that track the user's personal inflation rate over a window and comparison period the user picks. An increase in spending shows as a positive percentage in red, and a decrease as a negative percentage in green. Users can see whether their spending is rising faster than they want and adjust their habits.
- **[PR #124](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/124) – Add net worth percentage change to report and widget.** Adds a `totalChangePercent` value to the net worth spreadsheet and shows it next to the dollar change in the Net Worth report and dashboard widget. Users can see how significant a change is, not just its dollar amount.
- **[PR #129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129) – Bulk edit schedules.** Adds checkboxes and a bulk actions menu to the Schedules page, so several active schedules can be posted, skipped, completed or deleted at once, as on the Rules, Payees and Tags pages. Before, each schedule had to be changed one at a time through its row's "⋯" menu.
- **[PR #84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84) – Add option to change icon sizes.** Adds an accessibility setting for icon size. Users can make icons smaller to fit their window, or bigger to see them more easily.
- **[PR #112](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/112) – Add account color and description.** Users can give each account a color, as they already can for tags, so accounts are easy to tell apart. The color appears everywhere the account name is shown. Accounts also get a short description field, separate from Notes.
- **[PR #136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136) – Add live hex color preview and fixed "#" to tag color picker.** Replaces the picker's color field with a hex input that keeps "#" as a fixed prefix, so the tag color updates while typing. A preview swatch next to the input shows the typed color and stays in sync with swatch selection through `ColorPickerStateContext`.
- **[PR #144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144) – Add color picker to tag color editor (open, in review).** Clicking the color preview opens a saturation/brightness area and hue slider (react-aria-components), kept in sync with the swatches and hex input through the shared picker state. The reviewer requested changes, which will be addressed in Sprint 3.

**Bug fixes**

- **[PR #128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128) – Fix custom reports counting unchecked subcategories in their parent's total.** Fixes a bug from the Sprint 1 subcategories work: checking or unchecking a subcategory didn't change the chart. Now unchecked subcategories are left out, and the chart and parent totals update correctly.
- **[PR #132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) – Fix pinned sidebar closing context menus after leaving a popover.** With the sidebar pinned, context menus (such as a schedule row's "⋯" menu) closed on their own about 350 ms after the pointer left a popover. `SidebarProvider` now tracks popover hover only when the sidebar is floating. This also fixed the failing "schedules" E2E test.

**CI, testing and maintenance**

- **[PR #113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113) – Run CI on GitHub-hosted runners.** Moves CI from upstream's Depot runners, which are blocked on our repo, to GitHub's hosted runners. CI had never run on our PRs, which let bugs reach master. Also adds a checker script that fails if a Depot runner label comes back.
- **[PR #115](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/115) – Fix lint and knip errors in CI.** Fixes the formatting and lint errors that reached master while CI was down, and stops the formatter from rewriting `ai-logs/` and `docs/`. Also marks three Babel dependencies as used in `knip.json`, since knip wrongly reported them as unused.
- **[PR #116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116) – Update VRT screenshots for recent UI changes.** Regenerates 69 outdated VRT screenshots in CI's own Playwright container, using a temporary workflow that was removed before merging. Teammates later reused the workflow to generate screenshots for their own PRs.
- **[PR #104](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/104) – Fix failed mutation tests and pre-existing failed tests.** Fixes test failures that appeared when running `yarn test` locally, especially on Windows.
- **[PR #99](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/99) – Sync with upstream Actual v26.10.0.** Merges 215 commits from the upstream Actual Budget repo to keep our fork current, resolving 25 conflicts with our own changes.
- **[PR #140](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/140) – Verify layout and document narrow-screen behavior.** Adds tests that check layouts across viewport sizes, documents narrow-screen behavior, and lists next steps.

## Test Strategy

**Getting CI working came first.** Before [PR #113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113), CI had never run on our PRs, because upstream's workflows use Depot runners that are blocked on our repo. Lint errors, outdated screenshots and a broken E2E test had reached master as a result. After moving CI to GitHub-hosted runners, we fixed the failures that had piled up:

- [PR #115](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/115) fixed lint, formatting and knip errors.
- [PR #116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116) regenerated 69 outdated VRT screenshots.
- [PR #132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) fixed the bug behind the failing "schedules" E2E test.
- [PR #104](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/104) fixed tests that failed locally: Windows file locks, Vitest picking up Stryker's leftover `.stryker-tmp` copies, and an i18n race in `mutations.test.tsx`.

From then on, every PR got lint, typecheck, unit, E2E and VRT checks automatically.

**Kinds of tests written:**

- **Unit and component tests (Vitest)** were the most common.
  - [PR #84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84) tests saving and loading the icon size setting, the default fallback, and the pixel size for each option.
  - [PR #128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128) adds `subcategories.test.ts` and `showActivity.test.ts`, which check that unchecked subcategories are left out of custom reports.
  - [PR #132](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/132) adds three pinned-sidebar tests using fake timers, including a regression test for the original bug, and updates three existing tests.
  - [PR #136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136) adds six tests for the hex input.
  - PRs [#124](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/124) and [#130](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/130) add AI-generated unit tests for the net worth percentage and personal inflation features.
- **End-to-end tests (Playwright).**
  - [PR #129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129) tests bulk skip, complete and delete, select-all, completed rows having no checkbox, and clicking a row still opening the editor.
  - [PR #140](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/140) tests layouts at four viewport widths in three themes, plus a sweep across 19 widths. It records two known layout bugs with `test.fail()`, so they become regression tests once fixed.
- **Visual regression tests (VRT).** Screenshots were regenerated whenever a PR changed the UI ([PR #116](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/116), [PR #128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128), [PR #129](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/129)).
- **Mutation testing (Stryker).** In [PR #112](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/112), the changed code scored 100%, and each killed mutant was checked to be a real test failure.

**What we couldn't test automatically, and why:**

- **Upstream sync ([PR #99](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/99)).** It touched hundreds of files we didn't write, so no new tests could cover it. We ran the existing test suite and each teammate checked the app by hand for regressions before merging.
- **CI changes ([PR #113](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/113)).** A workflow can only be tested by running it on GitHub. We verified it by watching CI run on the PR, and tested the runner-label checker by hand against sample workflows.
- **How things look.** Whether icons look right at every size ([PR #84](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/84)) or colors look right in each theme ([PR #136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136), [PR #144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)) needs a person to look. VRT screenshots only catch changes, not whether the new look is correct.
- **Mutation testing on Windows.** Stryker's Vitest runner ran 0 tests on Windows and parallel runs crashed, so it had to be run one mutant at a time with temporary configs.
- **[PR #144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)'s unit tests** couldn't be run in the author's environment because Vitest wouldn't start. They rely on CI.

**Every PR was also tested by hand** in the running app. Several ([#128](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/128), [#130](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/130), [#136](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/136), [#144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)) include step-by-step instructions so the reviewer could repeat the check.

## AI Tool Usage

AI log folder: [`ai-logs/sprint2/`](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/tree/master/ai-logs/sprint2)

- **Liam:** For this sprint I used AI in a very similar manner to Sprint 1. I used Claude Code as an extension in Visual Studio, and used specstory to log them in my ai-logs like before. For PR descriptions and review comments, I would have AI type out responses, then I'd take the time to rewrite responses in my own words, though I didn't always do this. ## Risks & Retrospective

### What went well

- **15 of 16 issues merged.** The only open PR ([#144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144)) is finished apart from a few small requested changes.
- **CI works.** Every PR is now checked automatically. Before this sprint, CI had never run on our repo.
- **Our fork is current.** It is synced with upstream v26.10.0, and the test suite passes locally on everyone's machine, including Windows.
- **Reviews caught real problems.** Five PRs had changes requested before they were approved.

### What slowed us down

- **Other commitments.** Work for other classes and jobs was the biggest thing slowing us down, which led to a last-minute scramble. 7 of the 16 issues were closed in the final day of the sprint.
- **Unplanned infrastructure work.** Fixing CI and syncing with upstream took far longer than estimated (the upstream sync was estimated at 1 point). Feature PRs couldn't get green checks until it was done.
- **Slow CI runners.** GitHub's hosted runners are slower than upstream's Depot runners, so CI runs took longer and occasionally timed out.

### What we would do differently in Sprint 3

- Start PRs earlier so there is more time for review and for fixing the finer details. With PRs coming in at the last minute, some small details were skipped for the sake of finishing.
- Estimate infrastructure work (syncing, CI) more carefully. It turned out to be much larger than it looked.

### Risks going forward

- **Flaky CI.** Some CI tests occasionally fail because GitHub-hosted runners are much slower than upstream's Depot runners. Re-running a failed job usually passes, but we need to keep an eye on it and fix tests as the slowness comes up.
- **Config drift from upstream.** Our CI workflows, `.oxfmtrc.json` and `knip.json` now differ from upstream's, which may cause merge conflicts at the next upstream sync.
- **Known narrow-screen bug.** The layout bug found by PR #140 ([#139](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/139)) is still open.

## Sprint 3 Plan

- Address the review on [PR #144](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/pull/144) and merge it (carryover of [#67](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/67)).
- Polish the PDF export ([#97](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/97)). We planned this after Sprint 1 but didn't get to it this sprint.
- Show a "(modified)" label on report widgets with unsaved changes ([#125](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/125), [#126](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/126)).
- Fix the narrow-viewport layout bug ([#139](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/actual-budget/issues/139)).
- Add issues for bringing the UI changes we made in line with the project's "impeccable" design guidelines.
- Add screenshot tests for new UI elements that didn't have them before.
- Build a reliable way to update screenshots, like upstream's bot, so we no longer have to add and remove a temporary workflow each time.

# Committing Changes in actualbudget/actual

Before creating any git commit or pull request in this repo, read:

**`.github/agents/pr-and-commit-rules.md`**

It is the authoritative source for the rules you must apply yourself: the `[AI]` PR-title prefix and leaving the PR template blank (and the Chinese exception). The mechanical commit/git rules are enforced by tooling and aren't restated there. Read it on every commit/PR session so any updates are picked up automatically.

## The one rule worth restating

Every commit message and every pull request title MUST begin with `[AI]`. Commit messages are checked by the git-guard hook (a missing prefix is blocked before the commit lands), so the one that needs _your_ attention is the PR title — nothing checks it for you, and the cost of forgetting it is high since the PR has to be renamed by hand. Examples:

- `[AI] Fix type error in account validation` — correct
- `Fix type error in account validation` — wrong, missing prefix

The PR-template rule and the rest live in the rules file. Read it before each commit/PR rather than relying on this skill's summary, because the rules file evolves and this skill deliberately does not restate it.

## Why this matters

Maintainers triage AI-authored contributions separately, and the `[AI]` prefix is what makes that triage fast — it also drives the automatic `"AI generated"` PR label, so getting the prefix right is the one action that gates the whole triage path. Without it the PR looks like a normal human contribution and the wrong review process gets applied. The "do not fill in the PR template" rule exists because the human is the one who actually tested the change and can write the Description / Testing / Checklist sections honestly — an AI-filled template misrepresents who did what.

The rules file is short. Read it.
